options: Embryology is the morphological description of the transformations of the fertilized egg into an organism
Human embryology covers human development from the zygote stage until birth
Human embryology covers development from the zygote stage until puberty
The fetal period falls within the scope of human embryology
questions.explanation: Human embryology covers development from the zygote until birth, so it includes the fetal period. Puberty (secondary sexual characteristics) is mentioned only as the end of secondary/definitive morphogenesis, not as the limit of embryology.

questions.stem: About the cells defined in embryology:
options: The oocyte is a haploid sex cell with a single copy of each chromosome
The spermatozoon is a diploid cell that ensures fertilization
The zygote is a diploid cell resulting from the fusion of a male and a female gamete
A somatic cell is a haploid cell making up the body
questions.explanation: Both gametes (oocyte and spermatozoon) are haploid; the zygote and somatic cells are diploid.

options: Is a cell whose differentiation will produce a gamete
Is a germ cell
Is the diploid cell resulting from the fusion of two gametes
Is any cell making up the body of an organism
questions.explanation: A gonocyte is a germ cell whose differentiation produces a gamete. The fusion product of two gametes is the zygote; 'any cell making up the body' defines the somatic cell.

questions.stem: About the human virgin egg (female gamete):
options: It is a secondary oocyte (oocyte II) blocked in metaphase II
It is alecithal, i.e. devoid of nutritional reserves
Like the bird egg, it is very rich in vitellus
Vitellus (lecith) refers to the egg's nutritional reserves
questions.explanation: The human egg is an oocyte II blocked in metaphase II and is alecithal, unlike the bird egg which is very rich in vitellus (lecith = nutritional reserves).

questions.stem: The term 'germ' designates the developing organism:
options: From the 8th week of pregnancy until birth
As long as its shape is still spherical
Starting from the zygote stage
Until the end of the 3rd week of embryonic development
questions.explanation: 'Germ' is used while the shape is still spherical: from the zygote until the end of the 3rd week of development. From the 8th week until birth it is a fetus.

questions.stem: About the embryo and the fetus:
options: The embryo is the organism from the first division of the zygote until the main organs are sketched out
The fetus has bilateral symmetry
The fetal period is characterized essentially by the sketching out of the organs
During the first 8 weeks of pregnancy, we speak of an embryo
questions.explanation: Organs are sketched out during the embryonic period; the fetal period is characterized essentially by maturation and growth, since systems and organs are already formed.

questions.stem: An ultrasound is performed at the 14th week of pregnancy. At this stage, the developing organism:
options: Is designated by the term fetus
Is undergoing the first sketch of its neural tube
Grows and matures, its systems and organs being already formed
Is still called a germ because it is spherical
questions.explanation: From the 3rd month the organism has distinctive human characteristics and is called a fetus; the fetal period is mainly maturation and growth. The neural tube is first sketched in the 4th week, and 'germ' only applies until the end of the 3rd week.

questions.stem: About the section planes of the (spherical) germ:
options: The sub- and supra-equatorial planes pass through the animal and vegetative poles
They are similar to those used for the terrestrial globe
The meridian plane passes through the animal and vegetative poles
The equatorial plane cuts the germ into two equal parts
questions.explanation: Germ planes mimic the globe: the meridian plane passes through the two poles (animal and vegetative), the equatorial plane cuts it into two equal halves. Sub- and supra-equatorial sections lie below/above the equator, parallel to it, not through the poles.

questions.stem: About sections in the embryo and the fetus:
options: Longitudinal sections of the embryo are of 2 types: sagittal and para-sagittal
In the fetus, meridian and equatorial planes are used, as in the germ
Transverse sections can pass through any region of the embryo
In the fetus, bilateral symmetry being acquired, section planes are the same as in the adult
questions.explanation: The fetus has acquired bilateral symmetry, so adult section planes are used; meridian/equatorial planes belong to the spherical germ.

questions.stem: Which section necessarily divides the embryo into two equal parts?
options: The para-sagittal section
The transverse section
The sagittal (median) section
The sub-equatorial section
questions.explanation: The sagittal (median) section must pass through the embryo's axis of symmetry, giving 2 equal parts. The para-sagittal section is only parallel to it, and transverse sections can be at any level.

questions.stem: In this diagram of an embryo, the central black arrow, the two red arrows and the green arrow represent, respectively:
options: Para-sagittal, sagittal and transverse sections
Meridian, sub/supra-equatorial and equatorial planes
Sagittal, transverse and para-sagittal sections
Sagittal, para-sagittal and transverse sections
questions.explanation: The median longitudinal line through the axis of symmetry is the sagittal section, the lines parallel to it are para-sagittal, and the line perpendicular to the longitudinal plane is transverse. Meridian/equatorial planes apply to the spherical germ.

questions.stem: Fertilization, segmentation and the formation of the blastocyst belong to:
options: Primordial morphogenesis
Pre-morphogenesis
Primary morphogenesis
Secondary and definitive morphogenesis
questions.explanation: Pre-morphogenesis occupies the 1st week: fertilization, segmentation and blastocyst formation. Primordial morphogenesis (weeks 2–3) is the didermic → tridermic transformation.

options: It occurs during the 2nd and 3rd weeks of embryonic development
It corresponds to days 20–29 of pregnancy
It transforms the embryonic button into a didermic then a tridermic germ
Its process is gastrulation, leading to the gastrula stage
questions.explanation: Primordial morphogenesis (weeks 2–3) = gastrulation, producing a tridermic embryonic disc. Days 20–29 (4th week) correspond to primary morphogenesis.

options: It corresponds to the 4th week of pregnancy (20th–29th days)
Its characteristic stage is the gastrula
It ends with the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics
It establishes the first sketch of the nervous, circulatory and digestive systems
questions.explanation: Primary morphogenesis (4th week) is neurulation (neurula stage) and sets up the neural tube, circulatory and digestive sketches. The gastrula belongs to primordial morphogenesis; secondary sexual characteristics end secondary/definitive morphogenesis.

options: It ends at birth
It begins from the 5th week of pregnancy
It is when the different organs of the embryo are sketched out
It continues until the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics at puberty
questions.explanation: It starts at the 5th week and continues through the fetal period and even years after birth, until secondary sexual characteristics appear at puberty — so it does not end at birth.

questions.stem: A tri-dermic embryonic disc is the characteristic feature of which stage?
options: Zygote
Gastrula
Neurula
Embryo with organ sketches
questions.explanation: In the table of embryogenesis periods, gastrulation gives the gastrula, featuring a tri-dermic embryonic disc. The neurula features the neural sketch.

questions.stem: A woman is on day 24 of pregnancy. At this time, the conceptus is undergoing:
options: Formation of the blastocyst
Transformation of the embryonic button into a didermic germ
Neurulation, with the first sketch of the neural tube
The establishment of the first sketch of the circulatory and digestive systems
questions.explanation: Day 24 falls in the 4th week (days 20–29) = primary morphogenesis: neurulation plus first sketches of the circulatory and digestive systems. Blastocyst formation is 1st week; the didermic germ forms in weeks 2–3.
